bib.title: Human-Agent Interaction Patterns (Chapter 8, Agentic Architectural Patterns for Building Multi-Agent Systems)

question: Which architectural patterns govern the interface between humans and agents, and in what order should a team adopt them?
contributions: A five-level maturity model for adopting human-agent interaction patterns (Table 8.1)
Five patterns: Agent Calls Human, Human Delegates to Agent, Human Calls Agent, Agent Delegates to Agent, Agent Calls Proxy Agent
A four-tier integration architecture and a travel-booking chaining example

limits: No experiments or measurements; every number is an invented illustration (95% confidence, 1,800/1,500 sq ft, 6 months, 7 days, 3-month chart, delivery date 2025-09-22).
Table 8.2 metrics (escalation rate, resolution time, task success, CSAT/NPS, first-contact resolution, orchestration overhead, API error rate) name no targets or baselines.
Code is simulation: LLM calls, human review and HTTP are stubbed; human review returns a hard-coded decision.
Confidence threshold: no guidance on how agent confidence is computed or calibrated.
Timeouts and default actions on unanswered escalations are named but not shown.
Proxy example hard-codes a placeholder key ('SECRET_API_KEY') and the proxy is not itself secured against prompt injection.
No treatment of approval fatigue, permission scoping or reversibility of actions.
practices: Adopt patterns progressively by maturity level, not all at once (p.282).
Level 1 Human Calls Agent; 2 add Human Delegates and Agent Calls Human; 3 Agent Delegates to Agent; 4 Agent Calls Proxy Agent; 5 all patterns plus long-term memory (Table 8.1).
Separate tiers: UI, orchestration/primary agent, specialist workers, and an isolated security/proxy tier that alone holds external credentials (p.283).
Escalate when confidence is below a threshold, data is highly ambiguous, or policy requires human approval for a high-stakes decision (p.286).
On escalation, package state and context into a structured request and route it to a UI or task queue; pause the workflow until the decision returns (p.286).
Design the review UI to present context concisely and take structured input (buttons, forms) to minimize ambiguity (p.290).
Manage the paused state with timeouts and default actions if the human does not respond (p.290).
Use delegation for strategic ambiguity (agent plans) and escalation for new tactical ambiguity (agent asks) (p.291).
Add a Plan Confirmation go/no-go step before autonomous execution (p.295).
For Human Calls Agent, define tools with clear descriptions and strongly typed parameters so the LLM selects tools and extracts arguments correctly (p.298).
Orchestrator planning is the critical part: static sequences for predictable workflows, LLM-generated plans for dynamic ones (p.302).
Give the proxy agent sole network access and credentials for an external service; keep the primary-to-proxy protocol simple and standardized (p.307).
Instrument each pattern with metrics, for example log every escalation and time to human response (Table 8.2).

terms.definition: A formal escalation path for an agent to pause its operation, package the necessary context, and request a decision from a human expert
The user delegates a high-level, often ambiguous, objective; the agent plans, breaks it into sub-tasks and executes
A direct request-response cycle: classify intent, select the single best tool, execute, return the result concisely
A supervisor agent decomposes a goal and delegates sub-tasks to specialized worker agents, hiding the collaboration from the user
A specialized intermediary agent acts as a secure, standardized gateway to an external system and alone holds its credentials
Strategic ambiguity is a fuzzy high-level goal the agent resolves by planning; tactical ambiguity is an unforeseen problem during execution that triggers escalation
Orchestrating a team of internal agents
